spark.title: Performance vs. Scalability
spark.summary: Distinguish single-user latency optimization (performance) from proportional capacity growth under load (scalability), and know when to scale up vs. scale out.
spark.keyTakeaway: If a system is slow for a single user, you have a performance problem; if it is fast for a single user but slows down under heavy load, you have a scalability problem.
spark.byteSummary:
Distinguish single-user latency optimization (performance) from proportional capacity growth under load (scalability), and know when to scale up vs. scale out.

Teams routinely throw hardware or extra stateless replicas at a slow database query—only to watch p99 latency stay flat or worsen because lock contention and N+1 round trips are performance bugs, not capacity.

If a system is slow for a single user, you have a performance problem; if it is fast for a single user but slows down under heavy load, you have a scalability problem.

concept.whyItMatters: Teams routinely throw hardware or extra stateless replicas at a slow database query—only to watch p99 latency stay flat or worsen because lock contention and N+1 round trips are performance bugs, not capacity limits. Separating [Performance](/concept/latency-vs-throughput) from [Scalability](/domains/system-design) ensures you profile and fix algorithmic or I/O bottlenecks before sharding or auto-scaling.
whenToUse: Optimize performance first when single-request latency is high due to N+1 queries, unindexed scans, or synchronous serialization.
Scale horizontally (scale out) when single-request latency is fast at low load but saturates CPU, memory, or network I/O at peak QPS.
Scale vertically (scale up) temporarily for stateful monoliths or single-leader databases before investing in [sharding](/concept/database-sharding).
whenNotToUse: Adding more stateless web servers when the shared primary database connection pool is already saturated.
keyPoints: Performance measures how fast a single request completes under low load; scalability measures how well throughput and latency hold as load and resources increase proportionally.
Vertical scaling (scaling up) adds CPU/RAM/NVMe to one node—zero distributed complexity, but hits hardware ceilings and single-point-of-failure limits.
Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds commodity nodes behind a [load balancer](/concept/load-balancing)—requires stateless application tiers and partitioned state.
Amdahl's Law caps speedup when a serial bottleneck (like a global lock or single primary DB write) cannot be parallelized: $S_{\text{latency}}(s) = \frac{1}{(1 - p) + \frac{p}{s}}$.

sections.content:
## Architecture & Trade-Off Matrix

| Dimension | Performance Optimization | Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) | Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Root Problem** | Slow for 1 user | Fast for 1 user, hits single-node CPU/RAM cap | Fast for 1 user, needs >1 node capacity |
| **Mechanism** | Indexing, caching, async I/O, O(N) -> O(1) | Bigger instance (more cores/RAM/IOPS) | More nodes + [load balancer](/concept/load-balancing) + [sharding](/concept/database-sharding) |
| **Complexity** | Low (local code/query change) | Very low (no code change) | High (stateless design, distributed state) |
| **Ceiling** | Algorithmic lower bound | Hardware limit + single point of failure | Near-linear (until shared bottleneck) |
